paras: The attempted lynching of A. G. Adams was a failed attempt, in late September 1882 at Bonanza, Colorado, to lynch the cashier of the Bonanza Exchange Bank after his arrest following the bank's suspension. According to the single dispatch that reported it, the lynching was prevented by "some law-abiding citizens," and Adams was not reported harmed.

Adams was cashier of the Bonanza Exchange Bank, which had suspended payment a few days before the news went out. The reports name no charge against him, although the Omaha Bee headlined its item "Capture of a Runaway Banker" and said he had been "captured."

After the suspension Adams was arrested, and an attempt was then made to lynch him. The dispatch credited citizens it described as "law abiding" with stopping the attempt, and the Evening Star called it "ineffectual." No report describes the attackers, their number, the place or the hour, and the Kennebec Journal's shortened version spoke of "Attempts" in the plural without further detail.
No report of a charge, trial or any action against those who tried to lynch Adams was found in the coverage.

The story reached the white press as a Denver telegram of September 29 crediting the Denver Republican's special from Bonanza, and the Omaha Bee and Salt Lake Herald printed it on September 30. The same day the National Republican in Washington ran it under a headline about a try "to Lynch a Cashier," while the Evening Star and the Daily Kennebec Journal condensed it to a sentence or two.

In early October Midwestern weeklies reprinted it in roundups, the Mower County Transcript and Brookings County Sentinel under "Unfaithful Servants" beside an embezzling teller and the Worthington Advance among "Crimes and Criminals." The Rocky Mountain Husbandman carried the arrest but dropped the lynching attempt, and none of the papers mentioned Adams's race.

Most versions placed Bonanza in Colorado and named the cashier A. G. Adams, but the Evening Star put the bank in "Cal." and the Omaha Bee's text reads A. J. Adams. Because the story came through Denver from the Republican's Bonanza correspondent, the Colorado reading is the better supported.

bases: Every version reports only an attempt to lynch an arrested bank cashier that was prevented, with no killing or injury (A3, A4, A10).

Adams was not killed: the attempt was 'prevented by some law-abiding citizens' (A4, A10); the reports name no attackers, give no number, and state no motive beyond the bank's suspension and his arrest (A3, A6).

All versions are wire copies of one Denver Republican special from Bonanza, Colorado, credited as such by the Omaha Bee, Salt Lake Herald and Husbandman (A3, A4, A12); no independent or local account was found.
